definition: A program in execution, with its own address space, resources, and at least one thread of control.
wrongs: A single execution path that always shares its stack with every other path in the system.
A request that traps into the kernel to perform a privileged service.
A fixed-size block of a virtual address space.
why: The operating system tracks each process separately so one running program does not freely overwrite another.
example: Opening a browser and a text editor creates two running programs, each with its own memory.
scenario: A user opens a browser and an editor, and each has a separate address space. What is each running program?
scenarioWhy: Each running program with its own address space is a process.

definition: A schedulable path of execution that shares its process's address space with sibling paths.
wrongs: A program run with a private address space of its own.
A kernel record that stores a process id and saved registers.
A file-system object that maps names to files.
why: Threads of one process share code and the heap, while each keeps its own stack and registers.
example: One browser uses one execution path to draw the page and another to download a file, in the same memory.
scenario: Two downloads should share one browser's memory but run on separate stacks. What should be created inside that process?
scenarioWrongs: New page tables for each download
scenarioWhy: Threads share the process address space and keep separate stacks for the two downloads.

definition: The kernel record of a process's id, state, saved registers, and resource information.
wrongs: The cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.
The metadata record of a file's blocks and owner.
The queue of processes that are waiting only for the CPU.
why: The kernel saves and restores this record when it pauses one process and resumes another.
example: While an editor is paused, a kernel record still holds its process id and saved program counter.
scenario: The kernel must remember a paused editor's registers, state, and process id. Where is that information stored?
scenarioWhy: The process control block is the kernel record of a process's saved state and identity.

definition: Saving the processor state of the current process or thread and restoring another so it can run.
wrongs: A trap caused by touching a page that is not resident.
A controlled entry into the kernel to request a service.
A permanent wait cycle among processes holding resources.
why: The CPU is shared, so the outgoing registers are stored and the incoming ones are loaded.
example: When a time slice ends, the kernel saves the editor's registers and loads the browser's.
scenario: A time slice ends and the CPU must stop the editor and resume the browser. What is that changeover called?
scenarioWhy: Saving one process's CPU state and restoring another's is a context switch.

definition: A controlled entry into the kernel that lets a program request a privileged service.
wrongs: An ordinary call from one user function to another in the same program.
A hardware signal from a device that the program did not request.
A switch that saves one process and restores another.
why: User code cannot operate hardware directly, so it traps into the kernel to ask for the service.
example: A program's read request traps into the kernel, which copies bytes from a file into the user buffer.
scenario: A user program needs the kernel to read a file because it cannot touch the disk controller itself. What request does it make?
scenarioWhy: A system call is the program's controlled request for the kernel's read service.

definition: The processor privilege level in which privileged instructions and protected kernel memory are allowed.
wrongs: The restricted level used by ordinary applications.
A boot menu that starts the machine in a diagnostic shell.
A virtual-machine mode that only emulates an old processor.
why: The kernel runs at this level so it can manage hardware that user programs must not touch.
example: While handling a timer interrupt, the CPU may update the process table because it is fully privileged.
scenario: Code that updates the process table and masks interrupts must run with full hardware privileges. Which processor mode is required?
scenarioWhy: Updating the process table and masking interrupts are privileged operations of kernel mode.

definition: The restricted processor level for ordinary programs, where privileged instructions are forbidden.
wrongs: The level that may update the process table and talk to devices directly.
A mode used only while the bootloader is running.
A mode that disables all memory protection.
why: An attempt to execute a privileged instruction from this level traps instead of changing protected state.
example: A calculator runs without permission to execute a halt instruction that only the kernel may use.
scenario: A calculator must be prevented from executing a halt instruction reserved for the kernel. Which mode should it run in?
scenarioWhy: User mode forbids the halt instruction, so the calculator cannot execute it.

definition: The kernel's choice of which ready process or thread should use the processor next.
wrongs: The placement of virtual pages into physical frames.
The detection of a cycle of processes waiting for locks.
The allocation of disk blocks to a file.
why: A policy balances response time, fairness, and throughput when more ready work exists than processors.
example: After the running program blocks for disk, the kernel picks another ready program to run.
scenario: Several programs are ready and only one CPU is free. Which kernel activity assigns that CPU?
scenarioWhy: Choosing the next ready program for the CPU is scheduling.

definition: A scheduling policy that runs ready processes in the order they became ready.
wrongs: A policy that gives each process a fixed time slice in rotation.
A policy that runs the shortest CPU burst next.
A policy that always runs the best priority value next.
why: The ready queue is first-in first-out, so an early long job delays every shorter job behind it.
example: Jobs that became ready in the order A, then B, then C run all of A before B starts.
scenario: The ready queue must run jobs strictly in arrival order, even when a long job delays everyone behind it. Which policy is that?
scenarioWhy: Running in arrival order, with no time slice, is first-come first-served.

definition: A preemptive policy that lets each ready process run for a fixed time slice before the next process.
wrongs: A policy that runs processes only in the order they arrived, with no time slice.
A policy that always picks the shortest remaining burst.
A policy that never preempts the highest priority.
why: When the slice expires, the process moves to the tail of the ready queue and another process runs.
example: With a 10 millisecond slice, an editor runs briefly, then a browser runs briefly, and so on.
scenario: Interactive programs should take turns, each running about 10 milliseconds before going to the tail of the ready queue. Which policy is that?
scenarioWhy: A fixed time slice and rotation through the ready queue is round robin.

definition: A policy that runs next the ready process whose next CPU burst is the smallest.
wrongs: A policy that rotates equal time slices among ready processes.
A policy that runs processes in arrival order.
A policy that awards the CPU by random tickets.
why: Choosing the shortest burst first minimizes average waiting time when the burst lengths are known.
example: Among ready bursts of 8, 2, and 5 milliseconds, the burst of 2 milliseconds runs first.
scenario: The scheduler knows each job's next CPU burst and always picks the smallest one to cut average waiting time. Which policy is that?
scenarioWhy: Always selecting the smallest known CPU burst is shortest job first.

definition: A policy that runs the ready process with the best priority value ahead of the others.
wrongs: A policy that ignores rank and uses only arrival order.
A policy that gives every process the same time slice.
A policy that selects only by remaining burst length.
why: A better priority can outrank or preempt other work, and a poor priority can wait a long time if it never improves.
example: An audio task ranked ahead of a backup task runs first whenever both are ready.
scenario: An audio task must run before a backup task whenever both are ready, based on a numeric rank. Which policy is that?
scenarioWhy: Choosing the better numeric rank is priority scheduling.

definition: Taking the CPU away from a running process before that process blocks or exits.
wrongs: A voluntary pause in which the running process itself gives up the CPU.
A permanent wait in which processes hold one another's resources.
An indefinite delay of a low-rank process that is never selected.
why: A timer interrupt or the arrival of higher-priority work can force a switch so one job cannot hold the CPU indefinitely.
example: A timer interrupt stops a long compile so a newly ready interactive program can run.
scenario: A timer interrupt stops a long compile so the CPU can run a newly ready interactive program. What is that forced stop called?
scenarioWhy: The timer forces the compile off the CPU, which is preemption.

definition: A permanent wait in which each process holds resources that others need and none can continue.
wrongs: A long wait that ends once higher-priority work stops arriving.
A bug whose result depends on the interleaving of concurrent updates.
Heavy paging in which processes spend their time faulting.
why: Under the usual conditions, a cycle of waiting means none of the processes can make progress.
example: One process holds the scanner and waits for the printer, while another holds the printer and waits for the scanner.
scenario: Process A holds the scanner and waits for the printer, while B holds the printer and waits for the scanner. What is that state?
scenarioWhy: Each process waits for a resource the other holds, so both are deadlocked.

definition: The requirement that only one process at a time may use a particular non-shareable resource.
wrongs: A process holding some resources while it waits to acquire more.
A cycle of processes each waiting for the next process.
A rule that a resource can be released only by the process that holds it.
why: Some resources, such as a printer or a critical section, cannot be used correctly by two processes at once.
example: Only one process may send output to the printer device while other processes wait.
scenario: Two processes must not write the printer device at the same moment. Which deadlock condition is that requirement?
scenarioWhy: Allowing only one process to use the printer is mutual exclusion.

definition: A condition in which a process keeps at least one resource while waiting to acquire others.
wrongs: A requirement that a resource be used by only one process.
A cycle of waiting among several processes.
A rule that the operating system may seize a resource.
why: Keeping resources during a further wait lets waiting chains form.
example: A job continues to hold the scanner while it blocks requesting the printer.
scenario: A job keeps the scanner allocated while it blocks requesting the printer. Which deadlock condition is that?
scenarioWhy: Holding the scanner while waiting for the printer is hold and wait.

definition: A deadlock condition in which a resource is released only voluntarily by the process holding it.
wrongs: A requirement that only one process use a resource at a time.
A process holding one resource while requesting another.
A cycle in which each process waits for the next.
why: If the operating system cannot take the resource back, a waiting process cannot force the holder to give it up.
example: The kernel cannot seize the printer from the process that holds it; that process must release the printer itself.
scenario: The kernel is not allowed to take the printer away from the process that currently holds it. Which deadlock condition is that?
scenarioWhy: A resource that can be released only by its holder satisfies the no-preemption condition.

definition: A cycle of processes in which each process waits for a resource held by the next process.
wrongs: Exclusive use of a resource by one process.
Holding one resource while requesting another.
Voluntary release as the only way to give up a resource.
why: Together with the other Coffman conditions, this cycle means the processes are deadlocked.
example: A waits for B's printer, B waits for C's disk, and C waits for A's scanner.
scenario: A waits for a resource of B, B waits for a resource of C, and C waits for a resource of A. Which condition is that cycle?
scenarioWhy: A closed chain of waits is the circular-wait condition.

definition: A deadlock-avoidance test that grants a request only when some order can still finish every process.
wrongs: A scheduling policy that rotates fixed time slices.
A page-replacement policy that evicts the least recently used page.
A disk scheduler that sweeps the head in one direction.
why: Each process declares a maximum need, and the test looks for a safe sequence using those maxima.
example: The allocator refuses another tape to process A because no remaining order could then finish every process.
scenario: Before granting another tape, the system checks whether some order can still let every process finish. Which algorithm is that?
scenarioWhy: Granting a request only when a safe finishing order remains is the banker's algorithm.

definition: An integer synchronization object changed only by atomic wait and signal operations.
wrongs: A lock that records exactly one owning thread and ignores a count.
A busy loop that tests a flag without ever blocking.
A meeting point that releases threads only after a fixed number arrive, with no integer resource count.
why: Wait may block when the integer cannot be decreased under the semaphore's rule, and signal wakes a waiting thread.
example: An integer initialized to 3 allows at most three processes into a pool of shared buffers.
scenario: At most three processes may use a pool of buffers, tracked by an integer with atomic wait and signal. Which tool is that?
scenarioWhy: A counting semaphore initialized to 3 limits the buffer pool to three processes.

definition: A lock that only one thread may hold, used to protect a critical section.
wrongs: An integer that can allow several threads into a pool at once.
A lock that allows many readers while a writer waits.
A point that waits until every participating thread has arrived.
why: Only the thread that acquired the lock may release it, which gives mutual exclusion for the shared data.
example: A lock around a shared counter's increment stops two threads from updating that counter together.
scenario: A shared counter's update must be owned by only one thread, and only that owner may release the lock. What kind of lock is that?
scenarioWhy: A mutex has a single owner, which is what the counter update requires.

definition: Code that touches shared data and must not run concurrently with a conflicting execution of that code.
wrongs: A kernel entry used to request a privileged service.
The handler that runs after a device signal.
The startup code that loads the operating system.
why: One thread at a time should execute it so the shared update stays consistent.
example: The statements that read a balance, add a deposit, and store the result must not interleave with another thread.
scenario: The statements that read a balance, add a deposit, and store it must not interleave with another thread. What is that region of code?
scenarioWhy: Those shared balance updates form a critical section that must run exclusively.

definition: A bug in which the result depends on the unpredictable interleaving of concurrent operations.
wrongs: A permanent cycle of processes waiting for one another's resources.
An indefinite wait because higher-priority work keeps arriving.
A trap caused by a reference to a non-resident page.
why: Without synchronization, interleaved reads and writes can lose updates.
example: Two threads each read a balance of 100 and both write 110, so one deposit of 10 disappears.
scenario: Two threads each read balance 100 and both write 110, so one deposit disappears. What bug is that?
scenarioWhy: The lost deposit depends on the interleaving of the unsynchronized updates, which is a race.

definition: A construct that groups shared data with procedures that automatically exclude one another.
wrongs: An integer changed only by wait and signal, with no bundled data.
A busy-wait loop on a shared flag.
A synchronization point that releases threads only when all have arrived.
why: At most one thread runs inside it at a time, and condition variables let threads wait for a state change.
example: Buffer put and take operations exclude each other and wait when the buffer is full or empty.
scenario: Shared buffer operations should automatically exclude one another, with waits for full and empty. Which construct groups that data and those operations?
scenarioWhy: A monitor packages the buffer with mutually exclusive operations and condition waits.

definition: A memory scheme that divides logical and physical memory into fixed-size pages and frames.
wrongs: A scheme that divides a process into variable-sized logical regions such as code and stack.
A scheme that gives each process one contiguous block of physical memory.
A scheme that writes an entire process image to disk.
why: Any page can occupy any frame, which avoids the external fragmentation of variable-sized partitions.
example: A 4 KB piece of a process is stored in frame 12, and a table records that mapping.
scenario: Logical memory is split into fixed 4 KB blocks that may sit in any physical frame. Which scheme is that?
scenarioWhy: Fixed-size blocks placed in any frame are pages.

definition: A per-process structure that maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers.
wrongs: A cache of only the most recent address translations.
A file's metadata record of disk blocks.
The queue of processes waiting for the CPU.
why: The memory-management unit consults it, or a cache of it, on each address translation.
example: The entry for virtual page 5 says frame 20, so addresses in that page translate into frame 20.
scenario: The memory-management unit must find which frame holds virtual page 5 of a process. Which structure stores that mapping?
scenarioWhy: The page table entry for page 5 holds the frame number.

definition: A trap raised when a process references a virtual page that is not currently in physical memory.
wrongs: A deliberate kernel request made by a program to read a file.
A switch that saves one process and restores another.
An access that violates a segment limit and must kill the process.
why: The operating system can load the missing page, update the mapping, and restart the instruction.
example: The first touch of a newly reserved heap page traps, and the kernel supplies a frame of zeros.
scenario: A process touches a virtual page whose present bit is clear, so the kernel must load it. What is that trap?
scenarioWhy: A reference to a not-present page raises a page fault so the page can be loaded.

definition: A memory scheme that divides a process into variable-sized logical segments such as code, heap, and stack.
wrongs: A scheme of fixed-size blocks that can be placed in any frame.
A scheme that loads a page only on the first reference.
A scheme of equal fixed partitions assigned contiguously.
why: Each segment has its own base and limit, matching the logical parts of a program.
example: The code region and the stack region of one process have different base addresses and different lengths.
scenario: Code, heap, and stack should be separate variable-sized regions, each with its own base and limit. Which scheme is that?
scenarioWhy: Variable-sized logical regions with separate bases and limits are segments.

definition: A technique that gives a process a logical address space which need not all reside in physical memory.
wrongs: Allocation of one contiguous physical block large enough for the whole program.
Disk buffering of print jobs so programs need not wait for the printer.
Hardware transfer between a device and memory without further CPU copies.
why: Pages or segments are loaded as needed, so a program can be larger than the machine's RAM.
example: A program whose address space exceeds RAM still runs because only the pages it touches occupy frames.
scenario: A program's address space is larger than physical RAM, yet it runs because only active pages stay resident. What technique allows that?
scenarioWhy: Virtual memory lets the logical address space exceed the frames currently available.

definition: A small cache of recent page-table entries that speeds virtual-address translation.
wrongs: The full per-process table of every virtual page.
A cache of file data blocks read from disk.
A cache of inode metadata for path lookup.
why: A hit avoids walking the full page table in memory for that virtual page.
example: After the first access to page 5, later accesses use a cached translation and skip the in-memory table walk.
scenario: Repeated accesses to the same virtual page should avoid walking the page table in RAM every time. Which cache holds those recent translations?
scenarioWhy: The TLB caches recent page-table entries so translation can skip a full table walk.

definition: A state in which the system spends most of its time paging instead of executing useful instructions.
wrongs: A deadlock in which processes wait forever for one another's locks.
Starvation of one low-priority job while others run normally.
Wasted space inside an allocated fixed-size block.
why: Too many active processes compete for too few frames, so each runs only long enough to fault again.
example: Opening dozens of huge programs keeps the disk busy as each program immediately forces out another's pages.
scenario: The disk stays busy and processes make almost no progress because each runs only long enough to fault. What is that condition?
scenarioWhy: Continuous paging with almost no useful execution is thrashing.

definition: A policy that loads a page into memory only when a process first references it.
wrongs: A policy that loads every page of a process before it starts.
A policy that writes a whole process image out to disk.
A policy that divides memory into variable-sized logical regions.
why: Pages that are never touched occupy no frame, which is the usual way virtual memory is implemented.
example: A photo editor does not bring in a filter's page until the user actually applies that filter.
scenario: A large editor should not load a filter's page until the user applies that filter. Which loading policy is that?
scenarioWhy: Loading the filter page at the first reference is demand paging.

definition: A policy that evicts the resident page which has been in memory the longest.
wrongs: A policy that evicts the page whose most recent use is furthest in the past.
A policy that evicts the page which will not be used again for the longest future time.
A policy that gives a page a second chance if its reference bit is set.
why: Pages are ordered by arrival, and the oldest arrival is replaced even if it was used recently.
example: If pages arrived in the order 1, then 2, then 3, the next replacement removes page 1.
scenario: When a frame is needed, the system evicts the page that was loaded earliest, even if it was used a moment ago. Which policy is that?
scenarioWhy: Evicting the earliest-loaded page, regardless of recent use, is FIFO replacement.

definition: A page-replacement policy that evicts the page whose last reference is furthest in the past.
wrongs: A policy that evicts the page which has been resident the longest.
A policy that evicts the page unused for the longest time in the future.
A policy that chooses a resident page uniformly at random.
why: It approximates the idea that a page unused for a long time is less likely to be needed soon.
example: If page 2 was touched more recently than page 7, the next replacement removes page 7.
scenario: A frame is needed, and the system evicts the resident page that has gone unused for the longest time. Which policy is that?
scenarioWhy: Evicting the page with the oldest last use is least-recently-used replacement.

definition: The set of pages a process has referenced during a recent window of time.
wrongs: The entire virtual address space reserved for the process.
The cache of recent address translations.
The queue of processes that are ready to run.
why: Giving each process enough frames for this set makes thrashing less likely.
example: During the last 100 milliseconds a browser touched only pages 2, 5, and 9.
scenario: Over the last 100 milliseconds a process used only three pages, and the system tries to keep those pages resident. What is that set of pages?
scenarioWhy: The pages referenced in the recent window are the process's working set.

definition: The operating-system component that names, stores, and retrieves files on secondary storage.
wrongs: The component that chooses which ready process runs next.
The component that selects a victim page during a fault.
The component that looks for cycles in the lock-wait graph.
why: It maps file names and byte offsets to disk blocks and maintains directories and metadata.
example: Saving a notes file allocates disk blocks and records them under that file name.
scenario: A user saves notes.txt and later opens it by name, and the system finds the disk blocks for that name. Which component does that?
scenarioWhy: Naming a file and locating its disk blocks is the file system's job.

definition: A metadata record that stores a file's attributes and the locations of its data blocks.
wrongs: A directory entry that stores only a name and a pointer to metadata.
A small integer a process uses after opening a file.
A per-process map from virtual pages to frames.
why: The file name lives in a directory, while this record describes the owner, size, and block locations.
example: Record number 42 says a file has three blocks, is owned by user 1000, and lists those block addresses.
scenario: On a Unix-style system, a file's owner, size, and block addresses are stored apart from its name. What is that metadata record?
scenarioWhy: The inode holds the owner, size, and block pointers, while the name is stored separately.

definition: A file-system object that maps names to the files and subdirectories it contains.
wrongs: A metadata record of one file's blocks and owner.
An integer handle returned by a successful open.
A group of adjacent disk cylinders used for allocation.
why: Path lookup walks these objects from a starting point until the final name is resolved.
example: The folder /home/ada maps the name notes.txt to the metadata of that file.
scenario: The path /home/ada/notes.txt is resolved by looking up each name in the folder that contains it. What is each of those folders?
scenarioWhy: Each folder in the path is a directory that maps a name to the next file-system object.

definition: A small integer a process uses to refer to an open file in its private descriptor table.
wrongs: The metadata number that records a file's blocks on disk.
A virtual page number in an address translation.
The identifier of a running process.
why: After open succeeds, later reads and writes use this integer rather than the path name.
example: Opening a notes file returns 3, and a later read uses 3 rather than the path string.
scenario: After a successful open, a process reads a file using the integer 3 instead of the path. What is that integer?
scenarioWhy: The integer returned by open is the process's file descriptor for that open file.

definition: Wasted space inside an allocated block because the request was smaller than the block.
wrongs: Free space split into holes that are each too small for a request.
A system that pages so heavily it does little useful work.
A process that waits forever because others are always chosen first.
why: Fixed-size allocation rounds the request up, and the unused tail cannot be given to another request.
example: A 5 KB file stored in 4 KB blocks occupies two blocks and leaves 3 KB unused in the second block.
scenario: A 5 KB file occupies two 4 KB blocks and leaves 3 KB unused inside the last block. What is that waste called?
scenarioWhy: The unused tail inside the allocated block is internal fragmentation.

definition: Free space broken into holes that are too small to satisfy a request even though their total is enough.
wrongs: Unused space inside a block that was allocated larger than the request.
A process image written entirely out to secondary storage.
A cycle of processes waiting for one another's resources.
why: Variable-sized allocations can leave many free gaps, none of which fits the next request.
example: Three free holes of 10 KB cannot satisfy a 25 KB request even though 30 KB is free altogether.
scenario: Thirty kilobytes are free, but they are split into 10 KB holes, so a 25 KB request fails. What problem is that?
scenarioWhy: Enough free space exists in total, but no single hole is large enough, which is external fragmentation.

definition: Moving an entire process image between main memory and secondary storage.
wrongs: Loading a single page only when it is first referenced.
Buffering device output on disk so the requesting process can continue.
Keeping a copy of recent file blocks in memory.
why: Writing the whole image out frees all of that process's frames, and the image is read back when it runs again.
example: A suspended background program is written entirely to disk so a foreground program can use its frames.
scenario: The system writes a whole suspended process out to disk and later reads that entire image back. What is that movement?
scenarioWhy: Moving the entire process image out and back is swapping.

definition: The execution status of a process, such as new, ready, running, waiting, or terminated.
wrongs: The privilege level of the processor, such as kernel or user.
The name of the scheduling policy currently configured.
The set of pages referenced in a recent time window.
why: The scheduler and the wait queues move a process among these statuses as it runs and blocks.
example: A process that requests data from an empty pipe leaves the running status until data arrives.
scenario: A process that was running requests a read and must pause until data arrives. Which state should it enter?
scenarioWhy: A process blocked for data is in the waiting state, not ready or running.

definition: The set of processes that are in memory and are waiting only for a processor.
wrongs: The set of processes blocked for a device such as a disk.
The set of jobs that have been submitted but not yet admitted to memory.
The list of physical frames that are currently unused.
why: The scheduler selects the next process to run from this set.
example: After a disk read finishes, an editor moves from a device wait list onto the list of processes that need only the CPU.
scenario: A process is in memory, is not blocked on a device, and is waiting only for a CPU. Which queue should contain it?
scenarioWhy: A process waiting only for the CPU belongs on the ready queue.

definition: An asynchronous signal from a device or the timer that makes the CPU run a handler.
wrongs: A program's explicit request for a kernel service.
A fault caused by a missing virtual page.
A switch between two ready processes when a time slice ends, with no device signal.
why: Devices and the timer can get the kernel's attention without the CPU polling them continuously.
example: A disk controller signals that a read has finished, and the kernel runs the disk handler.
scenario: A disk controller signals that a read has finished, and the CPU immediately runs a handler. What is that signal?
scenarioWhy: The device's completion signal that invokes a handler is an interrupt.

definition: A situation in which a ready process waits indefinitely because other processes are always selected first.
wrongs: A cycle in which processes hold resources the others need.
A system that spends almost all of its time handling page faults.
A result that changes with the interleaving of unsynchronized writes.
why: Strict priority or shortest-job rules can keep a disadvantaged process from ever being chosen.
example: A low-priority backup stays ready for hours because new interactive tasks always outrank it.
scenario: A low-priority backup remains ready for hours because new interactive tasks are always chosen instead. What is that unfair wait?
scenarioWhy: The backup is ready but is never selected, which is starvation.

definition: Gradually raising the priority of a process that has been waiting for a long time.
wrongs: A situation in which a low-priority process holds a lock needed by a high-priority process.
Rotation of equal time slices with no priority change.
Writing a whole process out to disk because it is suspended.
why: The rising priority eventually makes the long-waiting process competitive, which prevents starvation.
example: A backup's rank improves a little every minute it waits, until the scheduler finally selects it.
scenario: A scheduler raises a waiting backup's priority a little every minute so the backup will eventually run. What is that technique?
scenarioWhy: Increasing priority with waiting time is aging.

definition: Buffering data for a slow exclusive device, such as a printer, so processes need not wait for the device.
wrongs: Moving an entire process between memory and disk.
Dividing memory into fixed-size pages and frames.
A condition in which the system spends its time paging.
why: Jobs are written to a spool, and a daemon sends them to the device in order.
example: Three programs write print jobs to disk and return at once, while the printer works through that queue.
scenario: Three editors submit print jobs and return immediately while a daemon feeds the printer from disk. What is that buffering called?
scenarioWhy: Queueing print output on disk so the editors need not wait for the printer is spooling.

definition: A system call that creates a child process by duplicating the calling process.
wrongs: A call that replaces the current process image with a new program.
A call that waits until a child process has terminated.
A call that ends the current process.
why: The child receives a copy of the parent's address space and continues from the return of this call.
example: A command interpreter duplicates itself, and the child then replaces its image with the program the user typed.
scenario: A shell must create a child that starts as a duplicate of itself before running a typed command. Which system call creates that child?
scenarioWhy: fork creates the duplicate child process; exec would replace a process image afterward.

definition: A terminated process whose exit status has not yet been collected by its parent.
wrongs: A process whose parent has already terminated, so it has been reparented.
A background process that has detached from its controlling terminal.
A path of execution that shares an address space with its siblings.
why: Its process record remains until the parent collects the exit status.
example: A child finishes, and until the shell collects the status the child entry remains with that status stored.
scenario: A child has exited, but its process entry remains until the parent collects the exit status. What is that child called?
scenarioWhy: A terminated child that still holds an unreaped exit status is a zombie.
